reason: The invariance claim is about the number found by counting a collection; counting.objects already presupposes the last-word idea (e9), so the dependence on last-word runs through counting.objects.
why: The claim that the count stays the same under any order or arrangement is about the total named by the last word, so that idea must already be in place.

reason: No, not as stated: Reading a written numeral requires mapping each numeral to its spoken name, including zero, but does not require reciting the entire count sequence in order.
why: Reading a numeral means saying the number word it stands for, so the learner must already know the spoken number words from one to nine.

reason: REJECT: Making one mark per object can be learned without first demonstrating one-word-per-object counting; the underlying correspondence idea is shared, but the specific skill is not mandatory.
why: Making exactly one mark for each car keeps every object paired once and none skipped or doubled, the same tagging discipline as one word per object.

reason: No, not as a universal prerequisite: Conceptual subitizing requires composing recognized parts into a whole, but count-all is only one possible route; count-on, known number bonds, and structured visual patterns are alternatives.
why: Knowing the whole the recognized parts make means finding the total of two sets joined together, the meaning of joining and counting all.

reason: The procedure counts each set and compares the counts; it can be run without understanding that spreading or reordering leaves the number unchanged. The invariance explains why spread is irrelevant and protects against the perceptual distractor in the test, but is not a step.
why: The comparison holds whatever the size or spread of the objects, because rearranging or spreading a collection does not change its count.

reason: REJECT: The line's starting end is supplied by the animals' orientation toward the barn, so relational position words need not be mastered first.
why: Identifying the stated starting end of a line (front, in front of, behind) uses position words; hedged, as the node could supply the end by pointing.

reason: The statement and test supply the sets already built ('put 3 counters on a plate, then add 2 more'); finding the total does not need the learner to build a set of a given size. Needed when addends are given as numbers, as in the story node, where it belongs.
why: Step one makes a first set of a given size, such as three counters, which is counting out a set of a given number.

reason: The statement and test have the starting set and the removal supplied; counting what remains does not require counting out a given number. Needed when the amounts are given as numbers, as in the take-from story node.
why: Steps one and two make the starting set and remove exactly the given number of objects, which requires counting out a given number.

reason: REJECT: The perceptual-comparison node is limited to very unequal sets; it is not a general prerequisite for reasoning that a whole contains more than a part.
why: The claim that the combined set has more than either part uses the idea of one collection having more than another.

reason: Dealing one at a time is executable without a check on equality; the matching idea justifies why the shares come out equal. Credit in the test is for 4 per bear made by dealing, not for the justification.
why: The check that shares are equal when every recipient received an object in the last round rests on pairing objects with recipients, so unpaired objects mean unequal.

reason: REJECT: Comparing two whole shapes does not invariably require counting their sides; a learner may directly overlay or visually compare corresponding parts.
why: The test asks the child to point to the part that does not match; the idea of a side as a part is assumed. Plausible, not certain.

reason: Joining sticks end to end creates the corners automatically. Knowing how many sides the shape has (e67) suffices to build it; corner knowledge helps check the figure but is not required.
why: The sticks must meet end to end at the corners, so the learner must know where the corners of the goal shape come.

reason: Dropped: the receptive shape-name node (replacing item 25's edge) tells the learner what the goal shape is; counting sides is not needed to build it. | Daniel: REJECT: A child can build a triangle from sticks through modeling or trial and error without first identifying and counting sides as a separate skill.
why: Each stick stands for one side of the shape, so the learner must know a shape's sides are straight segments and how many it has.

reason: REJECT for the assessed task: The test asks for a triangle from three sticks; comparing lengths is not a necessary prior skill for constructing that triangle.
why: If squares and rectangles are in scope, sticks must be chosen to be equal or paired lengths; the triangle test does not need it.

reason: Naming the triangles from a diagonal cut (right isosceles, turned) needs more than naming typical examples in usual orientation; the naming route runs through shapes.recognize, which itself builds on the names. Note that the test asks for naming and showing, stricter than the statement's 'or'.
why: The assessment asks the learner to name the smaller shapes the square splits into, such as two triangles.

reason: REJECT: A learner can discover how to turn or flip a piece through trial and error without previously mastering the separate skill of shape matching.
why: Choosing a turn, slide or flip to make a triangle fit requires seeing that the turned piece is the same shape as the outline.

reason: REJECT: A child can sort by color without naming the abstract attribute shared by a group.
why: Sorting by a stated attribute such as color requires treating color as one attribute with separate values and ignoring the other attributes like size.
